subject: Grouped intervals and problem with GOF

messages.author: 9650baa7f9da9041
messages.subject: Grouped intervals and problem with GOF
parts:
Dear distance sampling list,

 

I’m analyzing point transect data in distance to estimate abundance of a bird species. I have 190 sites in total that are divided in two strata (one with 74 sites and another 116). All sites were visited at least two times, but some of them received up to 5 visits and total effort was 619 and 102 observations. Data were collected in grouped intervals (0-50, 50-100, 100-200) and I used a global detection function, but stratified density. I read that when data is collected in grouped intervals each observation should be entered at the mid-point of the interval. So, this is how I entered it: 0-50 = 25; 50-100 = 75; 100-200= 150, so my intervals (bins) are 0, 50, 100, 200.

This is the first time that I analyze data that were collected in grouped intervals, and once I run models I can’t assess goodness of fit test, because I receive this message “No Degrees of Freedom for the test. No test possible”. I also get these warnings:

 * Warning: The number of intervals - 1 equals the number of key parameters   2 so no adjustments can be made. **

** Warning: The number of adjustment parameters allowed has   been reduced to  1 because of limited number of intervals. **

 

My problem is that since my data was collected as grouped intervals the only measure for goodness of fit left is the X2 test and I don’t know what I can do.

This is how my data look like.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Grouped intervals and problem with GOF
parts:
Fernanda

Collecting binned data means your data provide as many "points of support" as there are bins.  In your case, you have three bins.  The counts in the bins are "multinomial" meaning that if you tell me the total number of sightings (102) and the number of sightings in bins 1 (33) and 2 (31), then by subtraction I can tell you there were 38 sightings in bin 3.

As a result, the data you have collected possesses 2 degrees of freedom. 

The warnings produced by Distance can be interpreted in the context of these degrees of freedom.  The first message says "number of intervals minus 1" (2 in your case) is equal to the number of key parameters in the detection function model you wish to fit (hazard rate model has 2 parameters).  Consequently, no adjustment terms can be added to the hazard rate model.  The second warning states only a single adjustment term could be added to the detection function (presumably the half normal model with a single parameter).

Finally when the goodness of fit table is produced, you see a message stating there are no degrees of freedom remaining to compute the significance of the chi-square test statistic.  Note also that the agreement between the observed and predicted values in the chi-square table is perfect.

To have a degree of freedom remaining to perform the chi-square goodness of fit test, you will need to fit a detection function that does not have two parameters (all the degrees of freedom in your data)--namely the half-normal without adjustments.

Hi Eric,

Thank you for your prompt and detailed response. I ran the model as you suggested using a half-normal function with no adjustment terms and this is my GOF result.

Cell           Cut           Observed     Expected   Chi-square

Thank you,

Fernanda.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Grouped intervals and problem with GOF
parts:
Fernanda

With a small number of bins, as you have seen, you have limited ability to fit detection function and assess their fit.  Having a larger number of smaller width bins gives you more flexibility in your analysis.
